title: The Question That Caught BTK
central_question: How did one question to the police, and one deleted file, end a 31-year hunt for the BTK killer?

usa.source: Natural Earth 10m coastline, admin-0 land boundaries and admin-1 lines (public domain), naturalearthdata.com

content_notes: Non-graphic. No victims, crime scenes, violence or likeness of the perpetrator are shown. Objects (note, ad, disk, monitor, church) are labelled illustrations; no real document, newspaper page or photograph is imitated.

lines.text: A serial killer asked the police one question.
Could a floppy disk be traced?
They told him it was safe.
They lied.
From 1974, a killer who called himself BTK
murdered ten people in and around Wichita, Kansas.
He taunted police and the press with letters.
Then, for years, silence.
In 2004, he started writing again.
In January 2005, he left a note inside a cereal box.
"Can I communicate with Floppy and not be traced to a computer?"
If it was safe, he said, answer with an ad in the newspaper.
Police ran the ad:
"Rex, it will be OK."
Weeks later, a television station received a floppy disk from BTK.
Examiners found one deleted file.
Hidden in its data:
"Christ Lutheran Church."
And the name: "Dennis."
The president of that church's council was Dennis Rader.
A DNA test confirmed the link.
On February 25th, 2005, he was arrested.
He pleaded guilty to all ten murders.
Ten consecutive life sentences.
31 years of hiding,
ended by one question, one lie, and one deleted file.

claims.text: In a note left in a cereal box (location given by a postcard to KAKE-TV, 25 Jan 2005), BTK asked whether he could communicate by floppy disk without being traced: 'Can I communicate with Floppy and not be traced to a computer.' (wording as reported; minor variants exist)
He asked police to answer through a classified ad in The Wichita Eagle.
Police ran the ad 'Rex, it will be OK', signalling (falsely) that a disk could not be traced.
The reply was a deliberate deception by investigators; Rader later expressed shock that police had deceived him.
Between 1974 and 1991 BTK killed ten people in and around Wichita, Kansas (Rader pleaded guilty to ten counts of first-degree murder).
The killer used the name 'BTK' for himself in his communications.
In the 1970s BTK sent letters to police and the media; communications then stopped for decades until 2004.
In March 2004 BTK resumed communication with a letter to The Wichita Eagle, followed by further messages and packages.
In January 2005 a note from BTK was left inside a cereal box; a postcard to KAKE-TV gave its location.
Weeks later (16 Feb 2005 per AP) a floppy disk from BTK arrived at Wichita TV station KSAS.
Forensic examination found a deleted Microsoft Word document on the disk.
The deleted file's metadata named 'Christ Lutheran Church' and a user 'Dennis'.
Dennis Rader was president of the Christ Lutheran Church council.
Before the arrest, a familial DNA test (using a medical sample of his daughter's, obtained with court authorisation) linked him to crime-scene DNA.
On 27 June 2005 Rader pleaded guilty to ten counts of first-degree murder.
On 18 August 2005 he was sentenced to ten consecutive life terms (minimum 175 years).
From the first killings (January 1974) to the arrest (February 2005) is 31 years.
